title: Competition and Resource Partitioning Core Test
description: Use resource-use models and controlled comparisons to explain competition and how differences in resource use can reduce overlap.

questions.prompt: Two seedlings use water from the same small pot during a dry week. What makes competition for water possible?
questions.questionText: Two seedlings use water from the same small pot during a dry week. What makes competition for water possible?
options: They must belong to different species.
They must touch each other above ground.
Both need a shared supply that may be insufficient.
They must actively choose to fight.
questions.correctAnswer: Both need a shared supply that may be insufficient.
questions.explanation: Competition can occur when use by one organism reduces a resource available to another.

questions.prompt: Which is a resource plants can compete for?
questions.questionText: Which is a resource plants can compete for?
options: The name assigned to their habitat.
The age of the measuring ruler.
The number of observations in a notebook.
Light reaching their leaves.
questions.correctAnswer: Light reaching their leaves.
questions.explanation: Light is a resource used in photosynthesis, and shading can reduce its availability.

questions.prompt: Two birds of the same species use the few remaining nesting cavities. Can they compete?
questions.questionText: Two birds of the same species use the few remaining nesting cavities. Can they compete?
options: No; competition requires different species.
Yes; competition can occur within a species.
Only if they eat different foods.
Only if one bird eats the other.
questions.correctAnswer: Yes; competition can occur within a species.
questions.explanation: Organisms of the same species can share limited requirements.

questions.prompt: A model shows shrub roots -> water uptake -> less soil water for nearby grass. Which interaction does it represent?
questions.questionText: A model shows shrub roots -> water uptake -> less soil water for nearby grass. Which interaction does it represent?
options: Competition through use of a shared resource.
Predation by the shrub on the grass.
Cooperation that necessarily benefits both plants.
Conversion of grass into shrub tissue.
questions.correctAnswer: Competition through use of a shared resource.
questions.explanation: One plant can affect another indirectly by reducing available water.

questions.prompt: Bird A feeds mostly high in trees; Bird B feeds mostly near the ground. How could this help them coexist?
questions.questionText: Bird A feeds mostly high in trees; Bird B feeds mostly near the ground. How could this help them coexist?
options: Different locations create unlimited food for both.
Different feeding locations may reduce overlap in resource use.
Both birds stop needing food.
They must now belong to the same species.
questions.correctAnswer: Different feeding locations may reduce overlap in resource use.
questions.explanation: Using different parts of a habitat can reduce, but need not eliminate, competition.

questions.prompt: What does resource partitioning describe?
questions.questionText: What does resource partitioning describe?
options: Organisms agreeing verbally to divide food fairly.
One organism consuming another.
Every organism receiving equal amounts of food.
Organisms using different portions, places, or times of resource availability.
questions.correctAnswer: Organisms using different portions, places, or times of resource availability.
questions.explanation: Partitioning is a pattern of resource use, not a conscious agreement or a guarantee of equal shares.

questions.prompt: In matched pots, seedlings grown with neighbors gain 4 cm; those grown alone gain 7 cm. What is the measured difference?
questions.questionText: In matched pots, seedlings grown with neighbors gain 4 cm; those grown alone gain 7 cm. What is the measured difference?
options: Seedlings alone gained 11 cm more.
Seedlings alone gained 3 cm more.
Seedlings with neighbors gained 3 cm more.
Both groups gained 4 cm.
questions.correctAnswer: Seedlings alone gained 3 cm more.
questions.explanation: The difference is 7 - 4 = 3 cm; the mechanism still needs investigation.

questions.prompt: Which setup best tests whether neighbors reduce water available to a plant?
questions.questionText: Which setup best tests whether neighbors reduce water available to a plant?
options: Compare crowded plants in shade with isolated plants in sun.
Compare different species in different pot sizes without measuring water.
Compare matched plants with and without neighbors, measuring soil water and growth under otherwise similar conditions.
Observe only one crowded pot after a storm.
questions.correctAnswer: Compare matched plants with and without neighbors, measuring soil water and growth under otherwise similar conditions.
questions.explanation: A matched comparison and water measurements help test the proposed resource pathway.

questions.prompt: Two species eat the same seed type, but seeds are abundant. What can be inferred?
questions.questionText: Two species eat the same seed type, but seeds are abundant. What can be inferred?
options: Their diets overlap, but strong competition has not been demonstrated.
Sharing a food always proves severe competition.
One species must disappear immediately.
They cannot compete under any future condition.
questions.correctAnswer: Their diets overlap, but strong competition has not been demonstrated.
questions.explanation: Overlap alone does not show that the resource currently limits either species.

questions.prompt: A tall plant shades a shorter plant. Which chain explains a possible growth effect?
questions.questionText: A tall plant shades a shorter plant. Which chain explains a possible growth effect?
options: Less light -> more photosynthesis -> guaranteed faster growth.
Less light -> less photosynthesis -> less material available for growth.
Shade -> roots stop absorbing every mineral immediately.
Shade -> the shorter plant loses all inherited information.
questions.correctAnswer: Less light -> less photosynthesis -> less material available for growth.
questions.explanation: Light limitation can reduce photosynthesis and growth; the effect depends on conditions.

questions.prompt: A table shows A uses mostly large seeds and B mostly small seeds. Which model matches?
questions.questionText: A table shows A uses mostly large seeds and B mostly small seeds. Which model matches?
options: Partial separation by food size.
Complete separation by time of day.
Predation of A on B.
Identical use of every food size.
questions.correctAnswer: Partial separation by food size.
questions.explanation: Different food-size use is one kind of partitioning; the table says nothing about timing.

questions.prompt: Why might two species compete without meeting?
questions.questionText: Why might two species compete without meeting?
options: One can use a resource before the other reaches it.
Competition always requires direct contact.
Only animals can compete indirectly.
They must exchange signals first.
questions.correctAnswer: One can use a resource before the other reaches it.
questions.explanation: Using a shared resource at different times can still reduce what remains.

questions.prompt: A pond species feeds at dawn and another at dusk. What additional evidence is needed before claiming timing reduces competition?
questions.questionText: A pond species feeds at dawn and another at dusk. What additional evidence is needed before claiming timing reduces competition?
options: Whether the species names have different lengths.
Whether both were seen on the same calendar date.
Whether the pond has a single shoreline.
Whether enough food remains or is renewed between feeding periods.
questions.correctAnswer: Whether enough food remains or is renewed between feeding periods.
questions.explanation: Different times do not guarantee reduced competition if both exhaust the same food supply.

questions.prompt: A diagram shows two partly overlapping circles for food use. What does the overlap mean?
questions.questionText: A diagram shows two partly overlapping circles for food use. What does the overlap mean?
options: Some food types are used by both species.
The species have identical needs in every respect.
One species is necessarily eating the other.
All food outside the overlap is unusable.
questions.correctAnswer: Some food types are used by both species.
questions.explanation: Overlap represents shared resource use, not automatically competition intensity.

questions.prompt: In three matched pairs, plants alone gain 8, 7, and 9 cm; plants with neighbors gain 5, 4, and 6 cm. What supports a consistent neighbor effect?
questions.questionText: In three matched pairs, plants alone gain 8, 7, and 9 cm; plants with neighbors gain 5, 4, and 6 cm. What supports a consistent neighbor effect?
options: Only the tallest plant provides evidence.
The two groups have the same average growth.
Each pair differs by 3 cm in the same direction.
The pattern identifies water as the sole cause.
questions.correctAnswer: Each pair differs by 3 cm in the same direction.
questions.explanation: The repeated difference supports an effect, but resource measurements are needed to identify its cause.

questions.prompt: Shallow-rooted plants and deep-rooted plants share a field. Why might competition for water be reduced?
questions.questionText: Shallow-rooted plants and deep-rooted plants share a field. Why might competition for water be reduced?
options: Deep roots make the upper soil permanently wet.
Different root depths mean water is no longer limiting anywhere.
They may draw more water from different soil depths.
Plants with deep roots do not use water.
questions.correctAnswer: They may draw more water from different soil depths.
questions.explanation: Different access to a resource can reduce overlap, depending on where water is available.

questions.prompt: A student claims neighboring plants grew poorly because they competed for minerals. Which alternative should be checked?
questions.questionText: A student claims neighboring plants grew poorly because they competed for minerals. Which alternative should be checked?
options: The neighbors also shaded the measured plants.
All rulers used centimeters.
The samples were labeled before measurement.
The same notebook recorded both groups.
questions.correctAnswer: The neighbors also shaded the measured plants.
questions.explanation: Neighbor effects may involve light as well as minerals; measurements should distinguish causes.

questions.prompt: Both species use the same shelter and food. Food is added, but competition for shelter persists. What does this show?
questions.questionText: Both species use the same shelter and food. Food is added, but competition for shelter persists. What does this show?
options: More food must eliminate all competition.
Reducing one limitation does not remove every shared limitation.
Shelter cannot be a resource.
Adding food necessarily creates more shelter.
questions.correctAnswer: Reducing one limitation does not remove every shared limitation.
questions.explanation: Competition can involve multiple resources, so one improvement may leave another constraint.

questions.prompt: A bird's food-use counts are 18 small seeds and 2 large seeds; another's are 3 small and 17 large. What is the best description?
questions.questionText: A bird's food-use counts are 18 small seeds and 2 large seeds; another's are 3 small and 17 large. What is the best description?
options: Their seed use is identical.
Neither ever uses the other's common food.
The first bird consumes fewer total seeds.
Their use is mostly separated by seed size, with some overlap.
questions.correctAnswer: Their use is mostly separated by seed size, with some overlap.
questions.explanation: Both take 20 seeds, but their distributions differ; neither shows absolute separation.

questions.prompt: Which statement about an ecological niche is most accurate here?
questions.questionText: Which statement about an ecological niche is most accurate here?
options: It is only the map location where an organism was seen.
It is only the organism's body size.
It means every species uses a completely unique resource.
It includes how an organism uses resources and interacts with its environment.
questions.correctAnswer: It includes how an organism uses resources and interacts with its environment.
questions.explanation: Habitat is where an organism lives; niche includes resource use and interactions.

questions.prompt: Two species both grow poorly when together. Does that alone show which resource is limiting?
questions.questionText: Two species both grow poorly when together. Does that alone show which resource is limiting?
options: No; water, light, minerals, or other factors need investigation.
Yes; it must be water in every case.
Yes; it must be light because plants are green.
No; plant growth can never be measured scientifically.
questions.correctAnswer: No; water, light, minerals, or other factors need investigation.
questions.explanation: An interaction pattern does not by itself identify the mechanism.

questions.prompt: In a model, both species collect from the same 20 food tokens. Species A collects 12 and B collects 8. What happens if A takes 3 more before B, with no new tokens added?
questions.questionText: In a model, both species collect from the same 20 food tokens. Species A collects 12 and B collects 8. What happens if A takes 3 more before B, with no new tokens added?
options: At most 11 tokens remain for B.
B still has 8 because supplies are independent.
At most 5 tokens remain for B.
The total resource rises to 23.
questions.correctAnswer: At most 5 tokens remain for B.
questions.explanation: A would take 15 of 20, leaving 5; the finite shared supply links the outcomes.

questions.prompt: After a drought, shallow soil dries but deeper soil stays moist. Which prediction uses root-depth partitioning carefully?
questions.questionText: After a drought, shallow soil dries but deeper soil stays moist. Which prediction uses root-depth partitioning carefully?
options: Both groups must have identical access because they share a field.
Deep-rooted plants may retain access to water unavailable to shallow roots.
Shallow roots gain the advantage solely because they are shorter.
Deep roots guarantee survival regardless of other conditions.
questions.correctAnswer: Deep-rooted plants may retain access to water unavailable to shallow roots.
questions.explanation: Resource location affects access, while other limiting factors can still matter.

questions.prompt: A study removes neighboring shrubs, and grass grows faster. Why is a sham-treated comparison useful?
questions.questionText: A study removes neighboring shrubs, and grass grows faster. Why is a sham-treated comparison useful?
options: It proves grass cannot grow without shrubs.
It helps separate shrub removal from effects of soil disturbance during removal.
It removes the need for repeated sites.
It ensures every site has identical weather forever.
questions.correctAnswer: It helps separate shrub removal from effects of soil disturbance during removal.
questions.explanation: Handling or digging can affect growth, so comparable disturbance helps isolate the neighbor effect.

questions.prompt: Species A uses the upper canopy and B the lower canopy. After lower branches are removed, B feeds higher. What new interaction is plausible?
questions.questionText: Species A uses the upper canopy and B the lower canopy. After lower branches are removed, B feeds higher. What new interaction is plausible?
options: Overlap must decrease because there are fewer branches.
A and B stop sharing any food.
Greater feeding overlap may increase competition if food is limited.
B automatically becomes a predator of A.
questions.correctAnswer: Greater feeding overlap may increase competition if food is limited.
questions.explanation: Habitat changes can compress resource use into the same space.

questions.prompt: Crowded seedlings are smaller on average, but the pot has more total plant mass than a single-seedling pot. Is that contradictory?
questions.questionText: Crowded seedlings are smaller on average, but the pot has more total plant mass than a single-seedling pot. Is that contradictory?
options: No; more individuals can yield greater total mass while each is smaller.
Yes; lower individual growth always means lower total mass.
Yes; competition requires the total mass to be zero.
No; it proves the plants did not compete.
questions.correctAnswer: No; more individuals can yield greater total mass while each is smaller.
questions.explanation: Per-individual growth and group total are different quantities.

questions.prompt: A field study finds two species feeding in different areas. Which claim goes beyond the evidence?
questions.questionText: A field study finds two species feeding in different areas. Which claim goes beyond the evidence?
options: Their feeding locations differ.
The species consciously decided to share the field fairly.
Their use of space may reduce resource overlap.
Additional observations could test whether the pattern persists.
questions.correctAnswer: The species consciously decided to share the field fairly.
questions.explanation: Observed separation does not establish intention or agreement.

questions.prompt: Matched plants with neighbors gain 3 cm under low water and 6 cm under high water; plants alone gain 7 cm under both. What is the strongest interpretation?
questions.questionText: Matched plants with neighbors gain 3 cm under low water and 6 cm under high water; plants alone gain 7 cm under both. What is the strongest interpretation?
options: Water fully explains every difference because both groups are now equal.
Water has no possible role because plants alone did not change.
Neighbors necessarily improve growth under every watering level.
Extra water reduced the growth gap, supporting water as one contributor.
questions.correctAnswer: Extra water reduced the growth gap, supporting water as one contributor.
questions.explanation: The gap shrinks from 4 to 1 cm but does not disappear, so other effects may remain.

questions.prompt: A model predicts coexistence because two species eat different foods. A new study finds both depend on very scarce shelter. How should the model change?
questions.questionText: A model predicts coexistence because two species eat different foods. A new study finds both depend on very scarce shelter. How should the model change?
options: Keep only diet because one partitioned resource settles the issue.
Assume shelter becomes unlimited when diets differ.
Include the shared shelter limitation alongside diet differences.
Remove all resource information because the prediction is uncertain.
questions.correctAnswer: Include the shared shelter limitation alongside diet differences.
questions.explanation: A model must include important shared requirements beyond the first resource examined.

questions.prompt: A drought-year survey finds fewer plants where shrubs are dense. Which conclusion is most defensible without an experiment?
questions.questionText: A drought-year survey finds fewer plants where shrubs are dense. Which conclusion is most defensible without an experiment?
options: Shrubs certainly caused every missing plant through water uptake.
Competition is impossible because no plants were moved.
The survey proves the same effect in every climate.
The pattern is consistent with competition, but soil and other site differences could also explain it.
questions.correctAnswer: The pattern is consistent with competition, but soil and other site differences could also explain it.
questions.explanation: Observational association can guide a hypothesis without isolating cause.
